questions.question: What is the Virtual DOM and why does React use it?
questions.answer: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI. React compares the new tree with the previous one, calculates the smallest set of changes, and updates the real DOM efficiently.

questions.question: Explain the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components in React.
questions.answer: Controlled components keep form state in React state and update via props and events. Uncontrolled components keep state in the DOM and are read through refs when needed.

questions.question: How would you improve the performance of a large React list?
questions.answer: Use virtualization, stable keys, memoized row components, pagination or infinite loading, avoid unnecessary state updates, and profile rendering bottlenecks before optimizing.

questions.question: Describe how you handle accessibility in a reusable component library.
questions.answer: Use semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, focus management, ARIA only when needed, sufficient contrast, visible focus states, screen reader testing, and automated accessibility checks.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to balance design fidelity with frontend performance.
questions.answer: A strong answer explains the constraints, trade-offs, measurement approach, collaboration with design, and the final performance and UX outcome.

questions.question: What problems does server-side rendering solve, and what trade-offs does it introduce?
questions.answer: SSR can improve first contentful paint, SEO, and perceived performance. Trade-offs include server cost, hydration complexity, caching concerns, and harder debugging.

questions.question: How does React reconciliation use keys?
questions.answer: Keys help React identify which list items changed, were added, or removed. Stable keys preserve component identity and prevent unnecessary remounting or state mix-ups.

questions.question: How do you debug a layout that breaks only on mobile devices?
questions.answer: Reproduce with device emulation or real devices, inspect computed styles, check viewport units, flexible grid constraints, overflow, touch targets, and responsive breakpoints.
